task.goal: Reduce abandoned library holds at a branch with limited shelf space.
hard_constraints: One librarian can spend 20 extra minutes daily; no new app or fees.
Keep patrons' borrowing choices private and allow phone-free pickup.
Track shelf occupancy, actual pickups and mistaken releases during a three-week trial.
task.available_resources: Printed hold slips and existing circulation timestamps.
task.expected_result: A practical hold workflow with error checks.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A clear collection deadline with checked daily release
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce the time uncollected holds occupy shelves by using one clearly stated collection window and a daily expiration check. If local policy permits, trial a modestly shorter window; otherwise, consistently enforce the existing window. This primarily recovers shelf space sooner: it may not increase pickups and could inconvenience patrons who need longer.

Use printed slips to record the ready date, exact collection deadline and an opaque claim code. Keep names and titles facing inward or behind the service desk. Give patrons the deadline on paper whenever possible, and allow collection using the branch’s normal identification procedure without a phone. Preserve existing accessibility exceptions and any promised collection period. Start the clock only when the branch’s normal ready-notification requirement has been met; a shelving timestamp alone does not establish notification.

Allocate the librarian’s extra 20 minutes daily: five minutes to count occupied shelf positions, ten to check and process expired holds, and five to reconcile exceptions and pickup totals. Before releasing anything, compare the item identifier, deadline and current circulation status. Separate uncertain cases for review rather than releasing them. Check status again immediately before completing a release. Record releases on a staff-only paper tally with enough identification to investigate errors.

Prerequisites are policy permission for any shorter window and reliable ready/deadline information. If either is absent, use this workflow solely to eliminate overdue shelf dwell. Stop shortening the window if additional checking or patron problems exceed the daily allowance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run for three weeks, alternating eligible holds between the current window and the proposed window using a predetermined allocation rule, if policy permits. Otherwise compare consistent daily clearance with available pretrial circulation records, acknowledging the weaker comparison. Count shelf occupancy at the same time daily; use existing checkout timestamps to count actual pickups and distinguish pickup from other hold removals. Record mistaken releases, including premature releases, overlooked extensions and releases against the wrong record; check every trial release against its recorded deadline and status. Allow each cohort its full collection window before final comparison. Reject the shorter window if occupancy does not improve, pickups fall materially, or mistaken releases increase. Lower occupancy alone does not establish success.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Give patrons a paper collection cue they can act on
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce forgotten pickups by making the collection plan concrete when a patron requests a hold in person. Using an existing printed hold slip, give them a small take-home reminder showing the branch, opening hours, normal collection-window rule and how to check readiness through existing branch channels. Ask them to write a likely collection day after readiness is confirmed. Explain that the reminder does not itself mean the item is ready and does not reserve an appointment.

The mechanism is a visible reminder plus a practical plan, rather than earlier expiration. This could increase actual pickups while leaving the usual collection entitlement intact. Its effect is uncertain: it mainly reaches people requesting holds in person and will not solve transport barriers or holds that patrons no longer want.

Keep titles and borrowing details off the take-home cue unless the patron explicitly requests them. Use an opaque claim code only if the existing workflow supports it; ordinary identification must remain sufficient for phone-free pickup. Keep the corresponding staff slip private. Do not create a public list of names, titles or collection intentions.

Use the extra 20 minutes daily for up to ten minutes of brief reminder conversations, five minutes counting shelf occupancy and five minutes reconciling pickups and releases. Limit enrollment to the number that fits that allowance. Normal deadlines remain unchanged. Before any expiration release, verify the item identifier, actual deadline, extensions and current circulation status, with a final status check immediately before release. Record discrepancies and hold uncertain items for review. This alternative requires printed slips that can be used as take-home cues and enough participating in-person requests; it requires no app, fee or additional messaging service.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During the three-week trial, assign successive eligible in-person requests to either the paper cue or usual service using a predetermined alternating rule. Track group membership on private staff slips. Count total shelf occupancy at a fixed daily time and mark occupied trial holds by group. From circulation timestamps, count actual pickups and time from readiness to pickup; log releases separately so they cannot inflate pickup totals. Audit trial releases against deadlines and extensions, and record every detected mistaken release and patron report. Compare groups only after equivalent collection opportunities; report late-ready holds separately. The idea is unsupported if the cue group shows no improvement in pickup rate or shelf dwell, or if its delivery and checks exceed 20 extra minutes daily. Small numbers and undetected release mistakes limit confidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Offer a brief, private check for holds patrons no longer want
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Remove unwanted holds through explicit patron cancellation during ordinary desk visits. After normal identity verification, offer an optional check: “Would you like to check whether you still want your outstanding holds?” Review details privately and cancel only the specific holds the patron identifies. For ready items, this frees shelf space immediately; for pending items, it prevents unnecessary shelf occupancy later. The mechanism is correcting stale demand, rather than shortening deadlines or reminding patrons to collect.

Use existing circulation records and printed slips. Confirm each selected item privately before cancellation, then match its record and item identifier before removing it from the shelf. Check current status and extensions immediately before release. Leave uncertain cases untouched. Keep a staff-only tally distinguishing patron-requested cancellations, expiration releases and actual pickups. No public names or titles, phone, app or fee is needed; ordinary identification remains sufficient for collection.

Allocate the extra 20 minutes to eight minutes of optional checks, seven minutes of cancellation verification and retrieval, and five minutes of measurement. Stop offering checks when that allowance is used. This assumes staff can view and cancel holds through the existing circulation workflow and that enough hold users visit the desk. It will miss patrons who never visit and cannot solve travel barriers. A cancellation is useful space recovery, but must not be counted as a pickup.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For three weeks, use a predetermined alternating rule to offer the check to eligible desk visitors or provide usual service. Record group assignment privately without recording reasons for cancellation. Count occupied shelf positions at the same time daily. Use circulation timestamps to count actual pickups, and separately tally ready-item cancellations and subsequent shelf arrivals where records permit. Record mistaken releases, including wrong-item cancellations and removal without explicit consent; reconcile every trial cancellation with its staff slip. Compare unwanted ready holds removed per eligible visitor and actual pickups between groups. If checks find almost no unwanted holds, exceed 20 minutes daily, or introduce release errors, the mechanism is unsuitable. Branch-wide occupancy changes alone would provide weak evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Make collection a quick retrieval transaction
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce abandonment caused by difficult collection by giving ready holds stable, numbered shelf positions behind the desk and allowing a brief pickup-only transaction whenever the desk is available. Keep a private printed index connecting each hold record to its position. Staff retrieve the item after normal identity verification and complete normal checkout. Patrons need neither a phone nor a claim code. Place names and titles inward and keep the index inaccessible to other patrons.

The mechanism is lowering the time and uncertainty involved in collection. It could help patrons who postpone returning because previous pickups were slow. It depends on retrieval or desk delay being a real barrier; it will not address forgotten holds or unwanted books. Do not promise a separate staffed lane or interrupt an ongoing transaction. Introduce the arrangement through a generic desk notice that reveals no borrowing details.

Use printed hold slips for the position index, maintaining it as part of ordinary shelving and retrieval. Spend the extra 20 minutes on up to ten minutes of index maintenance and spot checks, five minutes of occupancy counting, and five minutes of pickup and release reconciliation. This requires an existing shelf arrangement that can accommodate numbered positions and routine staff capacity for checkout. Before releasing expired holds, match the physical item, circulation record, deadline, extensions and current status; check status again immediately before release. Quarantine discrepancies for review.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: First inspect a small sample of ordinary pickups to establish whether finding items causes appreciable delay. If it does, run the numbered-position workflow for three weeks, comparing retrieval times with that initial sample. Count shelf occupancy at a fixed daily time and use existing circulation timestamps to count actual pickups and ready-to-pickup intervals. Keep releases separate from checkouts. Log and investigate every detected mistaken release, including errors caused by an outdated position index, using a staff-only paper record. Audit each trial release against its deadline and status. Reject the arrangement if retrieval does not become faster, maintenance exceeds the time allowance, or errors appear. Faster retrieval without improved pickups or shelf dwell supports convenience only; the before-and-after comparison cannot establish causation confidently.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Allow a trusted person to collect with specific patron authorization
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce abandoned holds caused by difficulty visiting the branch by offering collection through a patron-authorized person, if existing library policy permits it. The mechanism is substituting an available collector for an unavailable patron. It could help patrons facing transport, mobility or scheduling barriers; it will not address forgotten or unwanted holds.

First confirm that existing policy provides a usable authorization and checkout procedure. If it does not, this alternative is not ready to trial. During ordinary desk interactions, explain the option briefly and provide the required instructions on a printed slip. Participation is optional. Follow the existing procedure for recording authorization, checking the collector’s identity and determining which holds they may collect. Do not treat possession of a reminder slip alone as authorization. Patrons can still collect personally using normal identification, without a phone.

Explain that an authorized collector will see the items they collect. Obtain the patron’s specific permission for that disclosure; keep names, titles and authorization records out of public view. If the existing procedure cannot establish the permitted scope privately and reliably, leave the hold available for personal collection.

Allocate the extra 20 minutes daily to five minutes explaining and recording the option, five minutes checking authorizations, five minutes counting occupied shelf positions and five minutes reconciling pickups and releases. Cap offers when this allowance is exhausted. Before handing over an item, match its identifier, hold record and authorization. For expiration releases, verify the deadline, extensions and current status immediately before release. Set discrepancies aside for review.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For three weeks, alternately offer eligible desk visitors the collection option or usual service; honor any independently requested authorized collection in either group. Keep assignments and outcomes on private slips. Count shelf occupancy at the same time daily. Use circulation checkout timestamps to verify actual pickups, tallying personal and authorized collection separately from cancellations and expiration releases. Record mistaken releases, including unauthorized handovers, wrong items and premature expiration releases, and reconcile every trial handover with its authorization. Compare pickup proportions among holds with equivalent collection opportunities; report unresolved holds separately. The mechanism is unsupported if authorized collection is rarely used or offered patrons show no pickup improvement. Stop the trial procedure after an authorization failure. Small numbers, existing awareness of the option and undetected errors limit conclusions.

EXPAND.title: Privately clear holds patrons no longer want
EXPAND.proposal:
Use routine desk visits to identify unwanted holds and obtain explicit cancellation before they consume more shelf time. The librarian privately asks participating patrons whether they still want each outstanding hold, using the existing circulation record with its screen shielded from others. Patrons may keep everything, cancel named items, or decline the review. Silence never authorizes cancellation. This changes demand directly: a reminder or an expiration check cannot recover an unwanted hold until someone acts on it.

For each requested cancellation, confirm the specific item privately, verify its identifier and current hold status, and use the normal cancellation process. If already shelved, retrieve the matching item and check status again before releasing it. If not yet shelved, cancel only where the existing system supports this. Leave ambiguous records untouched for normal staff review. If an error is discovered, use the branch’s correction procedure and explain any lost queue position; restoration cannot be assumed.

The branch librarian owns a three-week trial. Use staff-only printed slips for allocation and audit notes, storing them securely under existing retention rules. No public lists, new app, fees or phone are needed; normal identification remains sufficient for pickup. Keep collection windows unchanged.

Reserve eight extra minutes daily for brief reviews, seven for retrieval and verification, and five for measurement. Stop enrolling patrons when that allowance is reached. Prerequisites are existing cancellation capability and enough routine desk visits. This will miss patrons who never visit, and may shift work to reshelving or transfers.
EXPAND.experiment:
Alternate eligible patrons between the private review and usual service, recording allocation before asking. During three weeks, count total occupied hold positions at the same time daily and record participant hold occupancy by group. Use circulation timestamps to count actual pickups separately from cancellations and expirations. Log every detected mistaken release, including unauthorized cancellations, and audit trial cancellations against the recorded authorization and item identifier.

Compare occupied shelf-days, actual pickups per enrolled patron, and extra staff minutes between groups, keeping ordinary deadline checks identical. This directly tests whether demand review adds benefit beyond deadline enforcement. Stop reviews after any unauthorized cancellation pending investigation, or if work exceeds 20 extra minutes daily. Reject expansion if shelf use does not improve, pickups decline without a corresponding reduction in patron-confirmed unwanted holds, or handling work exceeds capacity. Small participation and errors discovered after three weeks limit confidence.

EXPAND.title: Improved P0: A clear collection deadline with checked daily release
EXPAND.proposal:
This retains P0’s deadline-and-release mechanism: recover space by removing genuinely expired holds. The substantive improvement is to establish a verified deadline before an item enters the release queue and require an item-specific release record. Begin with the existing collection window; shorten it only if policy permits and the branch can verify when the required ready notification occurred. A circulation timestamp alone may not prove notification. This can reduce occupied shelf time without increasing actual pickups.

The branch librarian runs the workflow for three weeks. At shelving, put the exact authorized deadline on the staff-facing printed slip. Keep names and titles concealed. Preserve extensions, accessibility exceptions and previously promised deadlines. Patrons use ordinary identification for pickup without a phone; a reminder slip is optional.

Spend five extra minutes daily counting occupied shelf positions, ten checking expired items, and five reconciling pickups and errors. Before release, match the physical item identifier to the circulation record, check the deadline and exceptions, then recheck current status immediately before completing the transaction. Keep uncertain items secured for ordinary staff review. Record each release privately on its slip so a later complaint can be investigated.

Resources are existing slips, circulation records and secure staff storage. If notification evidence or policy permission is missing, enforce only deadlines already valid under existing policy; do not calculate a shorter entitlement from shelving time. If no valid deadline can be established, hand the case to normal review. For a mistaken release, initiate the branch’s correction procedure and record whether recovery succeeds; queue restoration is not assured.
EXPAND.experiment: Against P0 implemented with the same collection window, compare alternating trial days using its daily deadline check versus the improved item-specific verification. Never deliberately omit normal release safeguards. Track daily occupied positions at a fixed time, actual checkout timestamps for holds, and discovered mistaken releases, including errors reported later during the trial. Compare pickups per hold whose collection window ended, accounting separately for extensions. Also record minutes and unresolved exceptions. Stop the changed procedure if it exceeds 20 extra minutes or causes a mistaken release. Equal occupancy and pickups with more checking time would show no gain; fewer errors alone would support only the error-control improvement.

EXPAND.title: Prevent failed collections by checking that ready holds are retrievable
EXPAND.proposal:
Target an earlier operational failure: a patron arrives, but staff cannot find a supposedly ready hold. A small reconciliation sweep can prevent that failed visit from becoming an abandoned hold. This differs from reminders, cancellation reviews and deadline enforcement because it improves the branch’s ability to complete a pickup already attempted. Its value depends on retrieval failures actually occurring.

For three weeks, the branch librarian uses printed hold slips and existing circulation records to check a rotating section of the holds shelf. Match physical item identifiers, slip identifiers and current hold status; verify placement under the branch’s existing filing rule. Keep all names and titles concealed from public view. Correct an unambiguous filing mistake immediately. Secure an item with conflicting identifiers for ordinary staff review rather than guessing its recipient, releasing it or changing its deadline.

At any unsuccessful pickup attempt, staff use normal identification and check the circulation record before searching the relevant shelf section. Record a minimal staff-only exception on a slip. If the item is found, complete the normal checkout; if unresolved, hand it to the branch’s existing missing-item procedure. Give the patron a paper record of the unresolved request without borrowing details. A return visit and ordinary identification remain sufficient; no phone, app or fee is required.

Allocate eight extra minutes daily to the rotating sweep, seven to resolving retrieval exceptions, and five to occupancy and outcome tallies. Stop the sweep when that allowance is exhausted; ordinary service takes priority. The prerequisite is access to existing hold-status records and a usable filing rule. If records cannot be reconciled, restrict checks to physical placement against existing slips and refer discrepancies through normal procedures. This route will do little where forgetting or transport barriers dominate.
EXPAND.experiment: Use week one to tally ordinary failed retrievals and outcomes; introduce the sweep in weeks two and three. Each week, track fixed-time shelf occupancy, actual hold checkouts, mistaken releases, failed retrieval attempts, unresolved cases and extra minutes. Compare failed retrievals per pickup attempt and pickups per hold reaching its deadline, while noting differences in incoming volume. Stop if checking causes a mistaken release or repeatedly exceeds 20 extra minutes. No baseline retrieval failures, or unchanged pickups alongside added work, would undermine this route. Treat the short before-and-after comparison as a feasibility check, not proof of causation.
